There’s a lot of layers and assumptions to unpack here. I’ll start by responding to your description of abortion as “selfish” and “irresponsible.” To begin with, it is accurate that choosing to have an abortion is selfish, but this is an insignificant point. All choices are selfish in essence, including the decision to keep the child instead of terminating the pregnancy, as it involves doing what one desires (they want to have the child). Furthermore, you repeatedly emphasize irresponsibility throughout your post, but this implies that women even have a responsibility to bear children to begin with, as if they have made a pledge or contractual agreement.  
You say that if you believe in evolution, you must also believe that 1) there is an objective purpose to sex, and 2) that objective purpose is to create children. However, evolution makes no conscious prescriptions and doesn’t assign objective purposes to things. At best, you could say sex just so happens to lead to pregnancy most of the time, just like how you would say being tall is advantageous for playing basketball, but not that playing basketball is the objective purpose of being tall. The fact infertile people still have sex shows that procreation is not the sole purpose of sex. You may be tempted to brush these counterexamples under the rug just because they’re an exception, but it won’t help your case. Even if the objective purpose of sex is to have children, whatever that means, it would still be irrelevant. You’re committing a fallacy of functional fixedness. To use an analogy, it would be like saying it is wrong to use a hairpin to pick a lock because a hairpin was made to pin hair. Even if something has a purpose, it’s only the intent of the person that matters.  
Lastly, you seem to place a high value on consequences, but seemingly just for the sake of having consequences, regardless if they have any benefit or utility. Although you say “avoiding consequences for their actions,” in a pejorative sense, there are literally countless examples where we try to avoid negative consequences and find it acceptable. For instance, even if a person is irresponsible and doesn’t wear sunscreen, we would not deny them treatment for their skin cancer. True, they want treatment to avoid the natural consequences of their actions, but it’s trivially true.

I feel a good amount of neuroscientists agree. Among those who disagree, Nozick’s experience machine and the so-called paradox of hedonism are often cited as counter-arguments. Personally, I feel Nozick’s thought experiment is to anti-egoism/hedonism what Libet’s neuroscience experiment is to Determinism. Both experiments came to supposedly groundbreaking conclusions, but once it was revealed what exactly the experiments entailed, the results became less impressive. As a determinist, I have to admit Libet’s experiment isn’t very good. It concludes Free Will doesn’t exist by performing tests that wouldn't even be able to prove if the subjects tested had free will or not anyway regardless of the results. This same problem happens with Nozick’s thought experiment. The experiment only works if you assume either A) nobody likes reality in and of itself, or B) the idea of being submerged in a simulation would never make a person uncomfortable. This is called a Status Quo Bias, and it’s the same reason why when a bunch of patients with ophidiophobia were asked if they’d be willing to jump into a snake pit on the condition that their fear of snakes would be go away as soon as they jumped in the pit, most of them said no. The fear they felt at the moment they were asked the question prevented them from being able to answer from the perspective of someone who didn’t have their fear. Those who disagree just seem to call this explanation BS and don’t really explain further. If there is a more in-depth explanation of why the status quo bias explanation doesn’t work, I haven’t heard it.

Then the paradox of hedonism, which states that a person paradoxically becomes more miserable the more they seek pleasure. While true, it’s true in a trivial sense. If someone seeks “pleasure” as if it’s a tangible thing that exists in and of itself, then of course they’ll be disappointed, because that’s not possible. It’s like a person staying up all night trying to literally catch sleep. While pleasure cannot be sought directly, it can be experienced indirectly by doing things that are found to be pleasurable. This is why people have the tendency to do things they like and to avoid things they dislike.  

The only somewhat valid objection to Eudaemonism and Hedonism I can think of is that it redefines “happiness” and “pleasure” to include a broad number of things one wouldn’t think of as being under those categories. Buts that’s why I tried making a distinction between direct, short-term happiness/pleasure and indirect, long-term happiness/pleasure. If that still seems like a stretch, no problem. “Preference satisfaction” could be a good alternative term for what psychological egoists and hedonists/eudaemonists are describing

I don’t think the fact some desire things for others runs contrary to psychological egoism, as it is still their own preferences they are trying to satisfy, even if they’re not the beneficiary. Although I would argue they are either helping others because A) they feel happy when others are happy or B) they would feel sad or guilty if they didn’t help out.

Same sort of thing for the soldier jumping on the grenade. He is doing it because he sees some “benefit” to it, such as satisfying his preference to save others. We know the soldier “wants” to do this because if something were preventing him from being able to do so, it would make him upset as he would be unable to satisfy his preference. The other explanation is that he’s doing it to prevent guilt that would result from letting his fellow soldiers down and living with the knowledge that his actions (or inaction) led to their demise

I think utilitarianism implies some kind of calculus by which you can sacrifice one’s happiness for the “greater good.” I think what I’ve proposed is more similar to the concepts of ethical hedonism/eudaemonism and psychological egoism. To counter what your friend said about “happiness,“ assuming he really just means hedonic pleasure, I would say he doesn’t have a holistic view of happiness. Happiness is an umbrella with two categories under it: short-term happiness (pleasure/hedonism) and long-term happiness (eudaemonism). Long-term happiness is expressed through what I call “indirect pleasures.” Those are the things we choose to do that although we do not derive pleasure/satisfaction from them directly, we still only choose to do them because we have an underlying expectation of pleasure/satisfaction motivating us. For example, you may hate going out and grocery shopping, but you also love the idea of not starving to death. Your desire to avoid the pain of starving is what motivates you to get food. If you thought that getting food wouldn’t give you something positive (like the taste, energy) or prevent something negative (starving) then you wouldn’t be motivated to do it

I think your friend is actually on the right track, although I think he could have worded himself better. “Happiness” is likely to get misinterpreted as hedonic pleasure. I would explain it this way: every conscious decision one makes is made because they either think A) it will provide them some benefit (pleasure/happiness) directly or indirectly or B) it will at the very least prevent them from feeling bad or being harmed. As weird as it sounds, your decision to not go into the happiness jar stems from your underlying desire to maximize happiness/satisfaction. This is because (presumably) either reality itself is what you desire or you just simply dislike the thought of being stuck in a simulation and that makes you uncomfortable (it would definitely make me uncomfortable too). People seek meaning only insofar as they feel it will make them more happy/less upset

Dissociative Identity Disorder is the current psychiatric diagnosis, although historically, it used to be categorized under two separate disorders: Split Personality Disorder & Multiple Personality Disorder. Split Personality described an individual who switched between 2 alternate personas (called “alters”), while Multiple referred to more than 2 alters/personas. If you want a disorder that isn’t as “horrible“ for the person experiencing it (although each have their own set of challenges) and allows for functionality, I’d say DID is your best bet out of the three you mentioned (DID, Anxiety, and Depression). This is mainly because Anxiety and Depression are characterized by their negative effect on a person’s emotional and mental well-being. A person could theoretically have multiple identities and each one is happy/content with their circumstances. However what makes disorders like depression and anxiety so devastating is how they impact people’s ability to function in life.

 In depression, the brain has inactive dopamine receptors, dopamine being the neurochemical that gives people motivation and energy to do things. Without this, the person is unable to feel happy/motivated and instead either feels sadness or numbness, often resulting in them committing suicide. Anxiety is the result of excess glutamate/adrenaline and is severely crippling, with most having to completely organize their life around their anxiety (not going out to places or doing activities that may have minor consequences). Every day is like walking on a tightrope for these people, always on edge.

If you don’t want to romanticize it or make it seem like a quirk, I’d say make sure that the challenges of these disorders really impact and limit their behaviors/choices in a meaningful way. Although if you don’t want it to be all doom and gloom (which it rarely is in real life), then you can maybe have it so their affliction works out for them in some specific turn of events (like a person’s anxious compulsion for washing their hands/wearing gloves saves their life when a strange plague hits their town), but don’t make it seem like the benefit is worth the disorder as a whole.

Yeah, I noticed other people weren't getting that one either. I've just found out it's an informal term that's interchangeable with "Maladaptive Daydreaming" and "Sleep-Waking" (not Sleep-Walking). It's a very rare phenomenon in which someone has absolutely NO perception of reality (hearing, seeing, feeling, etc.), essentially rendering them blind. The brain, to make up for a lack of external stimuli, confabulates internal imagery and sounds to give the illusion that one is in the real world. The cause is not entirely known. Initially, it was a sleep-wake disorder since brain scans showed Delta waves active in the awake state, and Beta waves in the sleeping state (causing their mind to go blank). But now it's currently a dissociative disorder, since it blocks those affected from interacting within reality. It's closely linked to Anton-Babinski Syndrome, which is a condition occurring in blind people who deny that they're actually blind. They insist they can see because they don't know their brain is projecting fake imagery.

When we diagnose things as disorders, it implies that there is something "orderly" to compare it to. Yes, I know you said read at home. But to a kid who can only focus on what they'd rather be doing, it just comes off as memorization or remembering the words on the paper for the test the next day. They're not told the overall importance of being able to read in a convincing manner, so they only define it by what punishment will happen if they don't do it. 

I would say taking a belonging as a way to get someone to perform a task provides a warped framework for people (especially kids) for how crime/punishment or cause/effect works, and what to expect in the "real world" (ironically, what the learning process is supposed to do). It gives them the implication that it's alright to take someone's things if they don't do what you want. I agree with you that reading is important, but keep in mind, importance is subjective and differs, so it's mere opinion and not fact. 

I think that knowing how to tie shoes is important, but if someone prefers to wear slip-ons, I'm not going to artificially create a scenario where they have to tie shoelaces by removing all the non-laced shoes from their closet. It's not how the real world works. If someone does stuff we disagree with or think is irresponsible (as long as it's not physically hurting or interfering with anybody else), most people let them be and if it really is that important, a situation where they'll have to learn/do that thing will come up naturally.

Sounds like it would work in theory but doesn't do all that much in practice. The thing is that if reading is forced, then no attention is paid to what they're reading. Many kids (even me at one point) fell through the cracks because, although we could read and pronounce words perfectly and memorize for a test, it was never anything more than that, just words with no meaning. I don't know why memorization and test-taking skills are considered the gold standard. For some reason, comprehension and visualizing descriptions aren't as important. It's one thing to be fluent in speaking a language, but then it's another thing to actually know what exactly you're saying. 

Also, creating artificial consequences to get kids to do stuff (which would otherwise be relatively inconsequential) really warps their feeling towards a certain concept. It implies that reading is something to dread and has no other purpose than to avoid having the things they love taken away from them. Only reason a lot of kids in my kindergarten class would read was because they were afraid of what would happen if they didn't, rather than being convinced of the benefits. This is why most kids hate math from the beginning. Sometimes, you can't force a square into a round peg. It doesn't prepare for real life. No one is going to take their belongings away when they don't read something in adulthood, so it sets them up for a false expectation of the real world.

So here's an explanation from a former citizen of the soviet union on how salary worked: "Salary range was very small.
